questions.prompt: Given `int x = 5;`, which statement boxes `x` (allocates a heap object holding a copy of it)?

choices.text: `long y = x;`
`IComparable c = x;`
`var list = new List<int>(); list.Add(x);`
`Span<int> s = stackalloc int[1]; s[0] = x;`

sources.claim: Boxing is the process of converting a value type to the type object or to any interface type implemented by this value type; it allocates an object on the heap and copies the value into it.
sources.title: Boxing and Unboxing - C#

questions.explanation: Boxing is the conversion of a value type to `object` or to any interface type it implements, so assigning `x` to `IComparable` allocates a box and copies the value. The tempting wrong choice is `List<int>.Add`: the generic list stores `int` directly, so no box is created (boxing happens with `List<object>` or non-generic collections). The widening conversion to `long` and writing into a span are plain value copies.

choices.text: Prints `456`, then `s` is `456`
Prints `123`, then `s` is `123`
Prints `123`, then throws `InvalidCastException`
Prints `456`, then throws `InvalidCastException`

sources.claim: After boxing, changing the original value type does not change the boxed copy; unboxing to an incompatible type such as (short)o on a boxed int throws InvalidCastException.
sources.title: Boxing and Unboxing - C#

questions.explanation: Boxing copies the value, so the box keeps `123` after `i` changes. Unboxing must target the exact boxed value type: `(short)o` on a boxed `int` throws `InvalidCastException`. The tempting wrong answer is that `(short)o` works like the numeric conversion `(short)i`; it does not, because an unbox is a type check followed by a copy, not a numeric conversion.

sources.claim: If a value type contains a data member of a reference type, only the reference is copied when the value type instance is copied; the TaggedInteger example prints 0 [A, B] and 7 [A, B].
sources.title: Value types - C# reference

questions.explanation: Assigning a struct copies its fields. `Number` is copied by value, so `n1.Number` stays `0`. The `tags` field is a reference, so only the reference is copied and both structs share one list, which is why `B` shows up in `n1` too. The tempting answer `0 [A]` assumes a struct copy is a deep copy; it is not.

choices.text: `False`, because synthesized equality also compares the runtime type (`EqualityContract`)
`True`, because both variables are statically typed `Person` and every declared property value matches between them
`False`, because records silently fall back to reference equality as soon as any inheritance is involved in the hierarchy
It does not compile, because the compiler never defines `==` between two different derived record types

sources.claim: For records to be equal their run-time types must be equal; the Teacher/Student example with identical values compares False, and the compiler synthesizes an EqualityContract property.
sources.title: Records - C# reference

questions.explanation: For records, the compiler synthesizes `Equals`, `==` and an `EqualityContract` property; two records are equal only if their runtime types match and all members are equal. A `Teacher` and a `Student` differ in runtime type, so the result is `False` even though every value matches. It is still value equality (not reference equality): two `Teacher` instances with the same values would compare equal.

questions.prompt: A library built with `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` exposes `public int Len(string name) => name.Length;` and compiles with no warnings. A caller in a project with nullable disabled calls `Len(null)`. What happens?

choices.text: The caller fails to compile, because the parameter is declared non-nullable
The compiler injected a null check, so `ArgumentNullException` is thrown on entry
A `NullReferenceException` is thrown at `name.Length`; nothing checks for null at run time
The runtime substitutes `string.Empty`, so `Len` returns `0`

sources.claim: The runtime behavior of your program is unchanged; nullable reference types are entirely a compile-time feature, and string and string? are both represented by System.String.
sources.title: Nullable reference types - C#

questions.explanation: Nullable reference types are entirely a compile-time analysis: `string` and `string?` are the same runtime type and no checks are emitted. A caller in a disabled context gets no warnings and can pass `null`, which fails at `name.Length`. The tempting belief that the annotation adds an argument check is wrong; if you need one at a public boundary, write `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(name)` yourself.

questions.prompt: A team models an order as `public record Order(string Id, List<OrderLine> Lines);`, uses it as a value object, a dictionary key and in a `HashSet<Order>`, and copies it with `with` before editing lines. Explain what goes wrong and how you would fix it.

sources.claim: Init-only positional properties give shallow immutability; two records sharing the same array stay equal after the array is mutated, and with expressions produce a shallow copy.
sources.title: Records - C# reference

sources.claim: Record types are not appropriate as entity types in EF Core, which depends on reference equality.
sources.title: Records - C# reference

questions.explanation: A senior answer names the mechanism (synthesized member-wise equality plus shallow copying), shows the shared-mutation bug with `with`, and proposes a fix that keeps hash codes stable for keys, instead of just saying 'records are immutable'.

model_answer.summary: Record equality is synthesized per member and is shallow, so a `List<T>` member is compared by reference, mutations through shared lists go undetected, and `with` shares the list; use an immutable collection with custom equality or a different model.
key_points: Synthesized `Equals`/`GetHashCode` compare each member with its own equality, so two orders with identical line contents but different `List` instances are not equal.
Positional properties of a `record class` are init-only, but immutability is shallow: the list contents can still be mutated, and two records sharing one list stay equal after a mutation.
`with` makes a shallow copy, so the copy and the original share the same `List`; editing the copy's lines silently edits the original, including any instance already used as a key.

Fix: expose an immutable collection and override `Equals`/`GetHashCode` to compare sequences, or keep collections out of the equality members; do not use such records as EF Core entities, which rely on reference equality.

questions.prompt: On a hot path, someone proposes turning a small mutable `class Point { public int X, Y; }` into a `struct` to avoid allocations. Explain the trade-offs and describe two bugs that copy semantics can introduce.

sources.claim: A variable of a value type contains an instance of the type; on assignment, passing an argument to a method, and returning a method result, variable values are copied.
sources.title: Value types - C# reference

sources.claim: Boxing allocates an object instance on the heap and copies the value into the new object.
sources.title: Boxing and Unboxing - C#

questions.explanation: Strong answers connect the performance win (no allocation) to the correctness risks (lost mutations, shared reference fields, boxing copies) and conclude that mutable structs should be avoided.

model_answer.summary: A struct variable holds the instance itself, so assignment, argument passing and returns copy it; that avoids heap allocations but means mutations apply to copies, reference fields are shared, and interface/`object` use boxes a separate copy.
key_points: A value-type variable contains the instance; assignment, passing as an argument and returning from a method all copy it, which removes heap allocation and GC pressure for small types.
Bug 1: mutating a copy (a local copy, a method parameter, a value returned from a property or collection) does not change the original, so updates are silently lost.
Bug 2: a struct holding a reference field copies only the reference, so 'copies' share the referenced object and mutations leak between them.
Converting the struct to `object` or an interface boxes it: the box is a separate copy, and it costs an allocation, which can erase the benefit.
Prefer small, immutable (`readonly`) structs; large structs cost more to copy than a reference.

questions.prompt: After enabling `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` and clearing every warning, a lead says `NullReferenceException` is now impossible in the codebase. Diagnose why that is wrong and say what you would still do.

sources.claim: Nullable reference types are entirely a compile-time feature; the ! operator suppresses warnings; default structs and new arrays of reference types can contain null without warnings; attributes such as NotNullWhen inform the analysis.
sources.title: Nullable reference types - C#

questions.explanation: A senior answer treats the annotations as documentation plus static analysis, lists concrete holes, and keeps runtime guards where untrusted callers enter.

model_answer.summary: Nullable reference types are a compile-time analysis with no runtime enforcement, and there are known holes, so nulls still flow in and public boundaries still need checks.
key_points: The feature is compile-time only: `string` and `string?` are the same runtime type and the program's runtime behavior is unchanged.
The null-forgiving operator `!` suppresses warnings without adding checks, and callers compiled with nullable disabled get no warnings at all.
Known holes: a `default` struct whose non-nullable reference fields are null, and arrays such as `new string[3]` whose elements start as null, produce no warnings.
Analysis does not look inside called method bodies, so helpers need attributes such as `[NotNullWhen(true)]` to be understood correctly.
Still validate arguments at public API boundaries (for example `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull`).

choices.text: All four parameters, including `name`, are captured as private fields of `Widget` itself, alongside the copy already held by `NamedItem`
`width`, `height` and `depth` become fields of `Widget`; `name` does not, since it only goes to the base constructor
`Widget` gets public `Width`, `Height` and `Depth` properties generated for it automatically, exactly the way a positional record type would
The parameters are in scope only inside field initializers and the base-constructor call, so referencing `width` from `Volume` fails to compile

sources.claim: Primary constructor parameters are captured in private fields only when they are used in members; a parameter used only to initialize fields or call a base constructor is not captured, and only records create public properties from them.
sources.title: Instance constructors - C#

questions.explanation: A primary constructor parameter is in scope in the whole type, but the compiler captures it as private state only when a member uses it. `name` is only used in the base constructor call, so `Widget` does not store it (the base class does). Only `record` types turn primary constructor parameters into public properties; a plain class does not, which is the tempting wrong choice.

choices.text: Prints `1`, exactly as before
Prints `2`
Throws `ArrayTypeMismatchException` at run time
Fails to compile with an ambiguity error

sources.claim: With C# 14, a covariant array passed to overloads taking IEnumerable<T> and Span<T> now binds to Span<T> and throws ArrayTypeMismatchException; workarounds are AsEnumerable() or a ReadOnlySpan overload.
sources.title: C# compiler breaking changes since C# 13

questions.explanation: C# 14 adds implicit span conversions, so `object[]` now converts to `Span<object>` and the `Span<T>` overload wins. Constructing a writable `Span<object>` over an array whose runtime type is `string[]` (array covariance) throws `ArrayTypeMismatchException`. The tempting answer 'prints 2' misses the covariance check. Workarounds: call `o.AsEnumerable()`, or add a `ReadOnlySpan<T>` overload, which is preferred and safe.

choices.text: `IEnumerable<int>.Generate(0, 10, 2)`
`new List<int>().Generate(0, 10, 2)`
Only as `SequenceExtensions.Generate(0, 10, 2)`; static extension members are not reachable through the extended type
It does not compile: an extension block must name its receiver parameter

sources.claim: An extension block with only a receiver type declares static extension members, which are called like static members of the receiver type, for example IEnumerable<int>.Generate(...).
sources.title: Extension member declarations - C# reference

questions.explanation: A receiver-only extension block (no parameter name) can declare static extension members, which are called as if they were static members of the extended type: `IEnumerable<int>.Generate(...)`. Instance-style calls need a named receiver, so `list.Generate(...)` is wrong. Naming the receiver is only required for instance members (and, in C# 15, extension indexers).

questions.prompt: A library team wants to rewrite its classic `this`-parameter extension methods as C# 14 `extension(...)` blocks. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: It is a binary breaking change, since the two syntaxes compile to different metadata shapes, so every downstream consumer must recompile
Extension blocks may be declared inside a generic static class, so the receiver's type parameters can simply move up onto the containing class
Each extension block introduces its own scope, so two separate blocks in the same class may declare members that share a signature
Both forms generate the same IL, so the move is binary and source compatible, but signatures must stay unique within the class

sources.claim: Both extension syntaxes generate the same IL, so moving between them is binary and source compatible; an extension block does not introduce a scope, and it must be declared in a top-level non-generic static class.
sources.title: Extension member declarations - C# reference

questions.explanation: The compiler emits the same metadata for both syntaxes, so migrating is neither a binary nor a source breaking change. An extension block does not introduce a scope: all members in the containing class, across blocks, must have unique signatures. Blocks must live in a top-level, non-generic static class, which rules out the generic-class option.

questions.prompt: Assembly A defines a C# 15 closed hierarchy: base class `Shape` with public derived types `Circle` and `Square`, and an `internal` derived type `Triangle`. Assembly B writes `shape switch { Circle c => ..., Square q => ... }` with no default arm. What does the compiler do in B?

choices.text: Treats the switch as exhaustive, since the internal `Triangle` type is not visible from assembly B at all
Reports error CS8510, since the compiler considers the two handled arms unreachable given the closed hierarchy
Reports warning CS8509: not exhaustive, since an internal direct descendant can't be handled
Compiles silently in B; the compiler only checks exhaustiveness for closed types once the program is actually running

sources.claim: A switch on a closed type is exhaustive when all direct descendants are handled; if a descendant is internal and not visible in another assembly, that assembly gets warning CS8509.
sources.title: Patterns - Pattern matching using the is and switch expressions. - C# reference

questions.explanation: A switch over a closed type is exhaustive without a default arm only when every direct descendant is handled. B cannot see or match the internal `Triangle`, so it gets warning CS8509 (and a runtime exception if a `Triangle` reaches the switch). The tempting idea that invisible types are ignored is wrong: they still exist at run time.

questions.prompt: Explain what the compiler generates for (1) a class primary constructor parameter that a method uses, and (2) a collection expression assigned to `IEnumerable<int>`, to `ReadOnlySpan<int>`, and an empty `[]`. What surprises follow in code review?

sources.claim: Primary constructor parameters are captured only when used in members; explicit constructors must call this(...); a class with a primary constructor has no implicit parameterless constructor.
sources.title: Instance constructors - C#

sources.claim: A collection expression always creates all its elements eagerly even when the target is IEnumerable<T>, distinct from LINQ; [] may use Array.Empty and a span target may be stack allocated.
sources.title: Collection expressions (Collection literals) - C# reference

questions.explanation: Senior answers explain the lowering (hidden fields, eager materialization, per-target storage) and turn it into review guidance, such as not using `[..query]` for lazy or huge sequences.

model_answer.summary: Primary constructor parameters become hidden private fields only when members use them; collection expressions are always built eagerly and the compiler chooses a storage strategy per target type.
key_points: A primary constructor parameter is in scope in the whole type and is captured as a hidden private field only when a member uses it; classes get no public properties from it (records do).
Once a class has a primary constructor, other constructors must chain to it with `this(...)`, and the class has no implicit parameterless constructor.
A collection expression always creates all its elements eagerly, even when the target is `IEnumerable<T>`; unlike a LINQ query it is not lazy and cannot be infinite.
The compiler may use `Array.Empty<T>()` for `[]` and may stack-allocate for a span target, so identity and mutability of the result should not be assumed.
Collection expressions cannot be constants or default parameter values.

questions.prompt: After moving a solution from `net8.0`/C# 12 to `net10.0`/C# 14: a test `Assert.Equal([2], x)` no longer compiles as ambiguous, a helper passing an `object[]` built from a `string[]` throws `ArrayTypeMismatchException`, and a property accessor that declares a local named `field` fails to build. Diagnose each and give fixes.

sources.claim: C# 14 span conversions make more overloads applicable and can cause ambiguity; covariant arrays can throw ArrayTypeMismatchException; field in an accessor binds to the synthesized field (CS9258) and a local named field is an error (CS9272).
sources.title: C# compiler breaking changes since C# 13

sources.claim: Using field in an accessor can clash with an existing member named field; disambiguate with @field or this.field.
sources.title: What's new in C# 14

questions.explanation: A strong answer traces each failure to the language change rather than patching symptoms, and knows the safe workaround (`ReadOnlySpan<T>` overloads, `@field`).

model_answer.summary: C# 14 adds implicit span conversions that change overload resolution, and makes `field` a contextual keyword inside accessors; each symptom follows from one of these.
key_points: C# 14 adds implicit conversions from arrays to `Span<T>`/`ReadOnlySpan<T>`, so span overloads now apply in more calls; the collection expression in `Assert.Equal` can now match several overloads, so make the target explicit (for example a typed array).
A covariant `object[]` over a `string[]` now binds to a `Span<T>` overload and throws `ArrayTypeMismatchException`; call `.AsEnumerable()` or add a `ReadOnlySpan<T>` overload.

Inside an accessor `field` now means the synthesized backing field: a local named `field` is error CS9272, and a reference to a member named `field` binds to the backing field with warning CS9258; rename it or use `@field` / `this.field`.
Also check array `Reverse()` calls: when targeting below `net10.0`, `x.Reverse()` can now bind to the in-place `MemoryExtensions.Reverse` instead of LINQ.

questions.prompt: Compare three ways to model a payment result so that `switch` expressions stay correct as cases are added: (a) an abstract base class with a `_` discard arm, (b) a C# 15 closed hierarchy, (c) a C# 15 union type `union PaymentResult(Approved, Declined, Pending)`. What does the compiler guarantee for each, and what traps remain?

sources.claim: A non-exhaustive switch expression gives a warning and a runtime exception; closed hierarchies are exhaustive when all direct descendants are handled; not has higher precedence than and, which is higher than or.
sources.title: Patterns - Pattern matching using the is and switch expressions. - C# reference

sources.claim: A union compiles to a struct with object? Value; value-type cases are boxed; a switch is exhaustive over the case types but needs a null arm when Value can be null, such as a default union.
sources.title: Union types - C# reference

questions.explanation: Senior answers weigh compile-time guarantees against runtime cost (boxing) and API evolution across assemblies, not just syntax.

model_answer.summary: A discard arm compiles but hides new cases; a closed hierarchy lets the compiler prove exhaustiveness over direct descendants; a union is exhaustive over its case types but is a struct wrapper that boxes value-type cases and can be default.
key_points: Abstract base + `_`: always compiles, but a newly added subtype silently falls into the discard; without the discard the compiler warns and an unhandled value throws at run time.

Closed hierarchy: the switch is exhaustive without a default arm when every direct descendant is handled; derivation is not transitive, so matching a base arm before a derived arm is flagged unreachable (CS8510), and an internal descendant in another assembly triggers CS8509.
Union: compiles to a struct exposing `object? Value`; patterns unwrap `Value`, value-type cases are boxed, and a `default` union has a null `Value`, so a `null` arm is needed for exhaustiveness.
Pattern precedence traps apply to all three: `not` binds tighter than `and`/`or`, so write `not (>= 'a' and <= 'z')` rather than `not >= 'a' and <= 'z'`.

questions.prompt: Which assignment compiles?

choices.text: `IEnumerable<object> a = new List<int>();`
`List<object> b = new List<string>();`
`IComparer<string> c = Comparer<object>.Default;`
`Action<object> d = (Action<string>)(x => Console.WriteLine(x));`

sources.claim: Variance applies only to generic interfaces and delegates and only to reference types; IComparer<T> and Action<T> are contravariant, and a value type argument makes the type parameter invariant.
sources.title: Covariance and Contravariance in Generics - .NET

questions.explanation: `IComparer<in T>` is contravariant, so a comparer of the base type `object` can be used where `IComparer<string>` is needed. Variance applies only to interfaces and delegates and only for reference type arguments: `List<T>` is a class (invariant), `int` is a value type so `IEnumerable<int>` is not an `IEnumerable<object>`, and `Action<in T>` only converts from `Action<Base>` to `Action<Derived>`, not the reverse.

choices.text: `True`, because the `class` constraint lets the compiler call `string`'s overloaded `==`
It does not compile, because `==` cannot be applied to a type parameter
`True`, because all equal strings are interned
`False`, because `==` on a `class`-constrained `T` tests reference identity

sources.claim: With where T : class, the == and != operators on T test reference identity, not value equality, even if the type overloads them; the OpEqualsTest string example prints false.
sources.title: Constraints on type parameters - C#

questions.explanation: Operators are bound at compile time. With `where T : class`, `==` is reference equality, even if the actual type overloads `==`. `s2` is a different string instance, so the result is `False`. Strings built at run time are not automatically interned, so the interning choice is wrong, and without the constraint `==` would not compile at all (except comparisons to `null`). Use `EqualityComparer<T>.Default` or `IEquatable<T>` for value equality in generic code.

choices.text: It throws `InvalidOperationException` because the collection was modified

sources.claim: A query variable stores the query, not the results; results depend on the data source at the time the query executes, and ToList or ToArray force immediate execution and cache the results.
sources.title: Introduction to LINQ Queries - C#

questions.explanation: `big` stores the query, not its results. It runs when `Count()` enumerates it, so it sees `{1, 2, 3, 4}` and counts `2, 3, 4`. The tempting answer `2` assumes `Where` ran on the first line. There is no 'collection modified' error because nothing was being enumerated when `Add` ran. Call `ToList()` to capture results at a point in time.

questions.prompt:
With EF Core, `StandardizeUrl` is an ordinary C# method:

```csharp
var blogs = ctx.Blogs
    .Where(b => StandardizeUrl(b.Url).Contains("dotnet"))
    .ToList();
```

What happens?

choices.text: It throws at run time: EF Core can't translate the method in `Where`, and client evaluation is only allowed in the final `Select`
EF Core silently loads the entire `Blogs` table into memory first and applies the `StandardizeUrl` filter there instead
It fails to compile, because an ordinary method call is not a legal node inside a lambda converted to an expression tree
EF Core inspects the method body at run time and translates `StandardizeUrl` into an equivalent user-defined SQL function

sources.claim: EF Core only supports client evaluation in the top-level projection; a Where with an untranslatable method such as StandardizeUrl throws at run time, and AsEnumerable or ToList explicitly opt into client evaluation.
sources.title: Client vs. Server Evaluation - EF Core

questions.explanation: The lambda becomes an expression tree, which the provider must translate to SQL. EF Core only evaluates untranslatable code on the client in the final projection (top-level `Select`); elsewhere it throws, to avoid silently pulling whole tables. Silent in-memory filtering was old EF Core 2.x behavior and is the tempting wrong choice. To do it on purpose, call `AsEnumerable()` or `ToList()` first and accept that the data is pulled to the client.

questions.prompt: A service published with `PublishTrimmed=true` calls `JsonSerializer.Serialize(order)` with no `JsonSerializerContext`. What happens by default?

choices.text: It works fine, because the trimmer statically detects every type reachable through `JsonSerializer.Serialize` and always keeps it
It throws `InvalidOperationException`, since reflection-based serialization is disabled by default in trimmed apps
It writes `{}`, because the trimmer removed `Order`'s properties but left the type itself and the serializer intact
It fails at compile time, because the build requires a source generator context for every serialized type once trimming is enabled

sources.claim: Reflection-based serialization is disabled by default when PublishTrimmed is enabled; with JsonSerializerIsReflectionEnabledByDefault false, using reflection-based serialization throws InvalidOperationException.
sources.title: How to use source generation in System.Text.Json - .NET

questions.explanation: Reflection-based System.Text.Json needs metadata the trimmer may remove, so it is turned off by default when trimming is enabled; calls that rely on it throw `InvalidOperationException`. The fix is a source-generated `JsonSerializerContext` with `[JsonSerializable(typeof(Order))]`, passed to the serializer. Believing the trimmer 'keeps what is used' is the misconception: reflection targets are not statically visible.

questions.prompt: `IEnumerable<Order> GetPending()` returns a LINQ query over a data source that makes a network call per enumeration. A caller writes `if (orders.Any()) { log.Info(orders.Count()); foreach (var o in orders) ... }`. Diagnose the problems and describe the fix.

sources.claim: Deferred queries may return different results each time they are enumerated; Count, Max and First execute immediately; OrderBy and GroupBy are nonstreaming operators; ToList and ToArray cache results.
sources.title: Introduction to LINQ Queries - C#

questions.explanation: A senior answer points out both the cost (repeated execution) and the correctness risk (inconsistent snapshots), and fixes the API contract, not just the call site.

model_answer.summary: The query is deferred, so each of `Any`, `Count` and `foreach` re-executes it, costing three round trips and risking inconsistent results; materialize once and return a collection type.
key_points: A query variable stores the query, not results; every enumeration re-runs it against the source.
`Any()` and `Count()` execute immediately and each enumerate again, so this code runs the query three times, with three network calls.
Results can differ between enumerations if the source changes, so the logged count may not match what the loop sees.
Nonstreaming operators such as `OrderBy` and `GroupBy` must read the whole source on every enumeration, which multiplies the cost.
Fix: materialize once with `ToList()`/`ToArray()` at the boundary and return `IReadOnlyList<Order>`, or make laziness explicit in the API.

questions.prompt: A repository method is `IEnumerable<Order> Find(Func<Order, bool> filter) => _ctx.Orders.Where(filter);`. After launch, database CPU and network traffic spike. Explain why, and compare it with taking an `Expression<Func<Order, bool>>`.

sources.claim: When a lambda is assigned to an Expression<TDelegate>, the compiler builds an expression tree that providers such as EF translate to SQL; statement lambdas and many constructs such as ?. and pattern matching cannot be used.
sources.title: Expression Trees - C#

sources.claim: Untranslatable expressions outside the top-level projection throw; captured instance methods or constants in client evaluation can cause memory leaks.
sources.title: Client vs. Server Evaluation - EF Core

questions.explanation: Strong candidates explain the overload resolution (Enumerable vs Queryable) that causes the silent client-side filter, and know the practical limits of expression trees.

model_answer.summary: A `Func` binds to `Enumerable.Where`, so EF sends an unfiltered query and filters in memory; an `Expression<Func<...>>` keeps `Queryable.Where`, so the provider translates the filter to SQL, within the limits of expression trees.
key_points: `Func<Order,bool>` can only bind to `Enumerable.Where`, so the `IQueryable` is treated as `IEnumerable`: the whole table is read and filtered on the client.
Assigning a lambda to `Expression<TDelegate>` builds an expression tree that `Queryable.Where` passes to the provider, which translates it to SQL.
Only expression lambdas become trees: statement lambdas and constructs such as `?.`, pattern matching and interpolated strings are not allowed in expression trees.
Untranslatable method calls outside the final `Select` throw at run time, so expression-based filters must stick to translatable operations.
Capturing instance members or constants in cached queries can cause memory leaks; prefer simple captured locals.

sources.title: How to use source generation in System.Text.Json - .NET

questions.explanation: A senior answer explains why reflection breaks with trimming/AOT (it isn't statically visible), and knows the concrete migration steps and gotchas, not just 'use source generators'.

model_answer.summary: Source generators run in the compiler and add code, moving the metadata work from runtime reflection to build time; System.Text.Json's `JsonSerializerContext` does this for JSON, with some rules and limits.
key_points: Source generators run during compilation, read the compilation (and additional files) and add new source to it, so work that reflection did at run time is done at build time.

For System.Text.Json, declare a `partial` class deriving from `JsonSerializerContext` with `[JsonSerializable(typeof(T))]` for each root type, and pass the context (or its type info) to the serializer.
Types that only appear at run time (for example through `object` properties) must also be declared, or serialization fails.
There are two modes: metadata-based and serialization-optimized (fast path); the fast path is not used for async serialization.
Reflection-based serialization is incompatible with Native AOT and trimming; for enums only the generic `JsonStringEnumConverter<TEnum>` works under AOT.

questions.prompt: It is September 2026. One service runs on .NET 8 (LTS) and another on .NET 9 (STS). When does support end for each?

choices.text: Both on November 10, 2026
.NET 8 in November 2027, .NET 9 in November 2026
.NET 9 in May 2026 (18 months), .NET 8 in November 2026
.NET 9 in November 2026, .NET 8 in November 2028

sources.claim: LTS releases are supported for three years and STS releases for two years; .NET 8 (LTS) and .NET 9 (STS) both end support on November 10, 2026, and .NET 10 (LTS) ends November 14, 2028.
sources.title: .NET and .NET Core Support Policy

questions.explanation: Under the current policy LTS releases get 3 years and STS releases get 2 years. .NET 8 shipped November 2023 and .NET 9 in November 2024, so both reach end of support on November 10, 2026. The '18 months for STS' figure is the outdated trap. November 2028 is the end date for .NET 10, the next LTS.

questions.prompt: A team's container image pins .NET runtime 10.0.2. Microsoft has since shipped 10.0.5. Is the team on a supported runtime?

choices.text: Yes, because .NET 10 as a whole major version is LTS and stays supported all the way until November 2028, regardless of the patch
Yes, but only for a grace period of six months after each new patch release ships, after which the older patch drops out of support
Yes, as long as the image comes from Microsoft's own official container registry rather than a third-party rebuild
No: support requires the latest patch, and patches are cumulative, so move to 10.0.5

sources.claim: You need to stay current with the latest patch update to remain supported; patches are released on Patch Tuesday and are cumulative.
sources.title: .NET and .NET Core Support Policy

questions.explanation: Support applies to the latest patch of a supported major version. Patches ship monthly on Patch Tuesday and are cumulative, so moving to 10.0.5 includes 10.0.3 and 10.0.4 fixes. The tempting answer confuses 'the major version is in support' with 'my runtime is supported'.

questions.prompt: A .NET Framework 4.8 app saves session blobs with `BinaryFormatter` and runs plugins in separate `AppDomain`s. What happens when it is ported to .NET 10?

choices.text: Both keep working unchanged if the project sets the old compatibility switch `EnableUnsafeBinaryFormatterSerialization` in its project file
`BinaryFormatter` throws on use with no opt-in switch, and `CreateDomain` throws `PlatformNotSupportedException`; use a safe serializer and processes for isolation

`BinaryFormatter` becomes safe once a `SerializationBinder` restricts which types it can construct, and `AppDomain`s are replaced automatically and transparently by `AssemblyLoadContext` with no code changes
Both fail to compile, because the `BinaryFormatter` and `AppDomain` APIs were removed entirely from the .NET 10 reference assemblies

sources.claim: BinaryFormatter is insecure and can't be made secure; starting in .NET 9 it throws on use and the compatibility settings were removed; SerializationBinder doesn't mitigate the risks.
sources.title: Deserialization risks in use of BinaryFormatter and related types - .NET

sources.claim: AppDomain creation isn't supported on .NET 6+ (CreateDomain throws PlatformNotSupportedException); use separate processes or containers for isolation and AssemblyLoadContext for dynamic loading.
sources.title: .NET Framework technologies unavailable on .NET 6+

questions.explanation: Starting with .NET 9, `BinaryFormatter` throws when used, and the old compatibility switches were removed. `AppDomain` creation is not supported on modern .NET: `AssemblyLoadContext` covers dynamic loading but is not a security or isolation boundary, so isolation needs separate processes or containers. A `SerializationBinder` does not make `BinaryFormatter` safe, which is the tempting half-truth in option c.

questions.prompt: A `BackgroundService` runs a synchronous database migration at the top of `ExecuteAsync`, before its first `await`, and the team relied on this finishing before other hosted services started. What changes on .NET 10?

choices.text: Nothing changes: the synchronous prefix before the first `await` still runs on the host's main startup thread, exactly as before
`ExecuteAsync` is now only invoked once the app has already started listening for requests, so the migration always runs too late to block anything meaningful
All of `ExecuteAsync` runs as a background `Task`; move the migration to `StartAsync` (before `base.StartAsync`) or `IHostedLifecycleService`
The host now throws a startup exception whenever `ExecuteAsync` blocks synchronously before reaching its first `await` expression

sources.claim: In .NET 10, BackgroundService runs all of ExecuteAsync on a background thread; previously the synchronous part before the first await ran on the main thread and blocked other services; move startup work to StartAsync before base.StartAsync or use IHostedLifecycleService.
sources.title: Breaking change: BackgroundService runs all of ExecuteAsync as a Task - .NET

questions.explanation: Before .NET 10 the synchronous prefix of `ExecuteAsync` ran on the startup thread and blocked the other services, which some apps relied on. In .NET 10 the whole method runs on a background thread. Work that must finish first belongs in the constructor, in an overridden `StartAsync` before calling the base, in `IHostedLifecycleService`, or in a plain `IHostedService`.

questions.prompt: Which ASP.NET Core app is the best fit for `PublishAot=true`?

choices.text: An MVC app that renders server-side Razor views and authenticates users with cookie-based authentication
A Blazor Server app that keeps its component state on the server over a persistent SignalR connection
An extensible app that loads third-party plugin assemblies at run time with `Assembly.LoadFile`
A minimal API using JWT bearer auth and a source-generated `JsonSerializerContext`

sources.claim: MVC, Blazor Server, Session and authentication other than JWT are not supported with Native AOT; minimal APIs are partially supported and JWT authentication is supported.
sources.title: ASP.NET Core support for Native AOT

sources.claim: Native AOT apps have no dynamic loading, for example Assembly.LoadFile.
sources.title: Native AOT deployment overview - .NET

questions.explanation: Native AOT supports minimal APIs (partially), JWT authentication, gRPC, CORS and similar features; the `webapiaot` template uses a `JsonSerializerContext`. MVC, Blazor Server, session and authentication schemes other than JWT are not supported. Native AOT also cannot load assemblies dynamically, so plugin loading with `Assembly.LoadFile` is out.

questions.prompt: You inherit a large ASP.NET MVC 5 app on .NET Framework 4.8: heavy `System.Web` use, several shared class libraries, WCF services and in-process session state. Leadership wants it on .NET 10 without a feature freeze. Outline your migration plan.

sources.claim: Incremental migration follows the Strangler Fig pattern and is recommended for large production apps with heavy System.Web use; libraries are upgraded in postorder depth-first order and multi-targeted; session and authentication are cross-cutting concerns to plan.
sources.title: Migrate from ASP.NET Framework to ASP.NET Core

sources.claim: Remoting, AppDomains, Code Access Security and WCF server are not available on .NET 6+; CoreWCF provides WCF server support.
sources.title: .NET Framework technologies unavailable on .NET 6+

questions.explanation: A senior answer is incremental and risk-aware (ship value while migrating), orders the dependency graph, and identifies blockers early instead of a big-bang rewrite.

model_answer.summary: Use an incremental (Strangler Fig) migration: stand up ASP.NET Core in front, move routes over gradually, upgrade libraries bottom-up with multi-targeting, and replace technologies that don't exist on modern .NET.
key_points: Choose incremental migration (Strangler Fig) for a large production app with heavy `System.Web` use; in-place migration only suits small apps.
Upgrade shared libraries in postorder depth-first order (leaves first), multi-targeting so both the old and new apps can consume them during the transition.
Plan cross-cutting concerns that both apps must share during the transition, such as session and authentication.
Replace unavailable technologies: WCF server through CoreWCF or another RPC stack, `AppDomain`/Remoting through processes and IPC, and `BinaryFormatter` through a safe serializer.
Use the current tooling (the GitHub Copilot app modernization agent); the .NET Upgrade Assistant is deprecated.

questions.prompt: You are leading a .NET 8 to .NET 10 upgrade of a solution with a web API, worker services and CI builds in containers. The build breaks with ambiguous-call errors on `Where`/`Select` over `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`. Explain that break and list other .NET 10 changes you would check before shipping.

sources.claim: System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable in .NET 10 is source incompatible with the System.Linq.Async package; remove it or upgrade to 7.0.0, use ExcludeAssets compile for transitive references, and SelectAwait becomes Select with an async lambda.
sources.title: Breaking change - System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable in .NET 10 - .NET

sources.claim: Breaking changes in .NET 10 include Ubuntu default container images, BackgroundService.ExecuteAsync running as a Task, dotnet restore auditing transitive packages, SLNX as the default solution format, and W3C as the default trace propagator.
sources.title: Breaking changes in .NET 10

questions.explanation: Strong answers group changes by risk (compile breaks, silent behavior changes, pipeline changes) and verify with tests rather than relying on the compiler alone.

model_answer.summary: The ambiguity comes from `System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable` moving into the core libraries and clashing with the community `System.Linq.Async` package; several other behavioral and tooling changes also need checking.
key_points: `System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable` is now in the core libraries and conflicts with the `System.Linq.Async` package: remove the package (or upgrade to 7.0.0), exclude a transitive reference with `<ExcludeAssets>compile</ExcludeAssets>`, and replace `SelectAwait` with `Select` using an async lambda.
C# 14 span conversions can change overload resolution in existing code.
`BackgroundService.ExecuteAsync` now runs entirely on a background thread, which changes startup ordering.
Default container images use Ubuntu, and `dotnet restore` now audits transitive packages, which can fail builds that treat warnings as errors.
Other defaults to check: `dotnet new sln` creates SLNX files, the default trace propagator is W3C, and configuration preserves null values.

questions.prompt: A team wants to publish an existing ASP.NET Core service with Native AOT to cut cold-start time in serverless containers. How do you evaluate feasibility, and what will break?

sources.claim: Native AOT limitations: no dynamic loading, no Reflection.Emit, trimming required, System.Linq.Expressions always interpreted, builds are per runtime identifier, and IsAotCompatible enables the analyzers.
sources.title: Native AOT deployment overview - .NET

sources.claim: Native AOT gives faster startup and smaller footprint; MVC, Blazor Server and Session aren't supported; CreateSlimBuilder omits HTTPS and HTTP/3; if there are no AOT warnings the app should behave like the JIT app.
sources.title: ASP.NET Core support for Native AOT

questions.explanation: A senior answer quantifies the benefit, audits dependencies for reflection, and uses the analyzers to make risks visible before production.

model_answer.summary: Native AOT gives faster startup and a smaller footprint but requires trimming and removes dynamic code; find problems with the AOT analyzers and treat every warning as a potential runtime failure.
key_points: Benefits: faster startup, smaller disk footprint and lower memory use, which suit scale-to-zero hosting.
Limits: no dynamic assembly loading, no `Reflection.Emit`, trimming is mandatory, and `System.Linq.Expressions` runs interpreted (slower).
ASP.NET Core limits: MVC, Blazor Server, session and non-JWT authentication are unsupported; minimal APIs need source-generated JSON; `CreateSlimBuilder` omits HTTPS and HTTP/3 by default.
Turn on `IsAotCompatible` / the AOT analyzers and fix every warning: warnings mean the app might not work, while a warning-free app should behave like the JIT version.
Builds are per runtime identifier, and a Linux binary only runs on the same or a newer distro version than the build machine.

questions.prompt: A team declares `public record Order(string Id, List<OrderLine> Lines);`, uses it as a dictionary key and in a `HashSet<Order>`, and copies it with `with` before editing lines. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Two orders with the same lines in different `List` instances aren't equal, since lists compare by reference
`Lines` is init-only, but the list it points to can still be changed after construction
The synthesized `Equals` compares the items in `Lines` one by one, so equal lines mean equal orders
`order with { Id = "B" }` copies only the list reference, so both records share one `List`
A `with` expression deep-clones every reference-type property, so the copy is independent

questions.explanation: Record equality compares each member with that member's own equality, so a `List<T>` member is compared by reference: equal contents in different lists aren't equal. Init-only properties are only shallowly immutable, so the list contents can still change, including in an instance already used as a key. A `with` expression makes a shallow copy, so the copy and the original share the same `List`. The synthesized `Equals` doesn't compare collection items, and `with` never deep-clones.

sources.title: Records - C# reference
sources.claim: Init-only properties have shallow immutability: the data a reference-type property refers to can be changed; the value-equality example shows two records sharing one array stay equal after it's mutated; the result of a with expression is a shallow copy, so the original and the copy reference the same instance.

questions.prompt: On a hot path, someone turns a small mutable `class Point { public int X, Y; }` into a `struct` to avoid allocations. Which statements about the change are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Assigning a `Point` to another variable or passing it to a method now copies the whole value
Setting `X` on a copy, such as a method parameter, no longer changes the caller's `Point`
A reference-type field inside the struct gets deep-copied as well whenever the struct is copied
Storing the struct in an `object` or interface variable boxes it into a separate heap copy
Boxing is free, because the box shares its memory with the original struct variable

questions.explanation: A value-type variable holds the instance itself, so assignment, argument passing and returns copy it, and a change to a copy doesn't reach the original. If the struct has a reference-type field, only the reference is copied, so the copies share that object. Converting to `object` or an interface boxes the value: a new heap object is allocated and the value copied into it, so the box and the original are separate and boxing costs an allocation.

sources.title: Value types - C# reference
sources.claim: On assignment, passing an argument and returning a result, value-type instances are copied, and operations on a value-type variable affect only that instance; if a value type contains a reference-type member, only the reference is copied.

sources.title: Boxing and Unboxing - C#
sources.claim: Boxing converts a value type to object or an interface it implements, allocating an object on the heap and copying the value into it; the original and the boxed object use separate memory locations, and boxing is computationally expensive.

questions.prompt: After enabling `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` and clearing every warning, a lead says `NullReferenceException` is now impossible in the codebase. Which statements show why that's wrong? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The feature is compile-time only, and `string` and `string?` are the same runtime type
`new string[3]` or a `default` struct can hold nulls in non-nullable references with no warning
The runtime inserts a null check before every dereference of a non-nullable reference
The null-forgiving operator `!` silences a warning without adding any check
The analysis traces into every called method's body, so helpers never need attributes

questions.explanation: Nullable reference types are entirely a compile-time feature: the runtime behavior is unchanged and `string?` is still `System.String`. Known pitfalls such as new arrays of references and `default` structs leave nulls in non-nullable references without a warning. The `!` operator just tells the compiler to trust you. The analysis doesn't look inside called methods, so helpers need attributes such as `[NotNullWhen(true)]`, and public APIs should still validate their arguments.

sources.title: Nullable reference types - C#
sources.claim: Nullable reference types are entirely a compile-time feature and the runtime behavior is unchanged; string and string? are both System.String; the null-forgiving operator overrides the analysis; the analysis doesn't trace into method bodies; default structs and new arrays can leave non-nullable references null without a warning.

questions.prompt: A code review covers a class primary constructor `class Widget(int width)` whose parameter a method uses, and collection expressions assigned to `IEnumerable<int>`, `ReadOnlySpan<int>` and an empty `[]`. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A parameter used inside a method is captured as a hidden private field, not a public property
A class primary constructor creates a public property for each parameter, as a record does
A collection expression for `IEnumerable<int>` creates all its elements eagerly, unlike LINQ
An empty `[]` may become `Array.Empty<T>()`, and a span target may be stack-allocated
A class with a primary constructor still gets an implicit parameterless constructor

questions.explanation: In a class, a primary constructor parameter that a member uses is captured as a private field; only records get public properties. A collection expression always builds every element into an in-memory collection, even for an `IEnumerable<T>` target, so it isn't lazy like a LINQ query. The compiler picks the storage: `[]` can be `Array.Empty<T>()` and a span may be stack-allocated, so don't rely on identity or mutability. A class with a primary constructor doesn't get an implicit parameterless constructor, and other constructors must call `this(...)`.

sources.title: Instance constructors - C#
sources.claim: Uses of a primary constructor parameter in other members cause the compiler to capture it in a private field; only record types get synthesized public properties; for class types the implicit parameterless constructor isn't emitted when a primary constructor is present, and other constructors must call this(...).

sources.title: Collection expressions (Collection literals) - C# reference
sources.claim: A collection expression always creates a collection with all its elements, even when the target is IEnumerable<T>, unlike LINQ; [] can be realized as Array.Empty<T>(), and a Span<T> or ReadOnlySpan<T> target might be stack allocated.

questions.prompt: After moving from `net8.0`/C# 12 to `net10.0`/C# 14, `Assert.Equal([2], x)` is ambiguous, a call passing an `object[]` built from a `string[]` throws, and an accessor declaring a local named `field` fails to build. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: C# 14's new span conversions make `Span<T>` overloads apply, so the old call can be ambiguous
The covariant array now binds to a `Span<T>` overload, which throws `ArrayTypeMismatchException`
Inside an accessor `field` is now a keyword, so rename the local or declare it as `@field`
Inside an accessor, `field` still binds to a class member named `field`, exactly as in C# 13
The exception is a runtime bug in `net10.0` that a later patch release is expected to fix

questions.explanation: C# 14 adds implicit span conversions, so `Span<T>`/`ReadOnlySpan<T>` overloads now apply in more calls; `Assert.Equal([2], x)` can match several overloads and become ambiguous, fixed with `x.AsSpan()`. A covariant `object[]` over a `string[]` can now bind to a `Span<T>` overload and throw `ArrayTypeMismatchException`; call `.AsEnumerable()` or add a `ReadOnlySpan<T>` overload. Inside an accessor `field` now means the synthesized backing field: a local named `field` is error CS9272, and a member named `field` binds to the backing field with warning CS9258. These are language changes, not runtime bugs.

sources.title: C# compiler breaking changes since C# 13
sources.claim: New span conversions can make calls such as Assert.Equal([2], x) ambiguous; a Span<T> overload chosen for a covariant array crashes with ArrayTypeMismatchException (workaround AsEnumerable); field in a property accessor refers to the synthesized backing field (warning CS9258), and a local named field is error CS9272 unless renamed or written @field.

sources.title: What's new in C# 14
sources.claim: C# 14 adds implicit conversions for Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T> and field-backed properties; in types with a symbol named field, use @field or this.field to disambiguate.

questions.prompt: A team compares three ways to model a payment result so `switch` expressions stay correct as cases are added: an abstract base with a `_` arm, a C# 15 `closed` hierarchy, and `union PaymentResult(Approved, Declined, Pending)`. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: With the abstract base and a `_` arm, a new subtype compiles silently and falls into the discard
A switch over a `closed` class needs no default arm once every direct descendant is handled
A `closed` class's exhaustive set includes indirect descendants, so each needs its own arm
A `default` union has a null `Value`, so the switch may also need a `null` arm
A union stores value-type cases without boxing, since the generated union type is a class

questions.explanation: A discard arm matches anything, so the switch keeps compiling and a new subtype quietly takes the discard path. For a `closed` class the compiler treats the switch as exhaustive when every direct descendant is handled; derivation isn't transitive, so indirect descendants aren't part of the exhaustive set and are covered by their base arm. A `union` declaration compiles to a struct with an `object? Value`: value-type cases are boxed, and a `default` union has a null `Value`, which must be handled to avoid a warning.

sources.title: Patterns - Pattern matching using the is and switch expressions. - C# reference
sources.claim: A discard pattern matches any expression; a switch over a closed class is exhaustive when its arms handle every direct descendant, and derivation from a closed class isn't transitive, so only direct descendants form the exhaustive set.

sources.title: Union types - C# reference
sources.claim: The compiler converts a union declaration to a struct with an object? Value property that always boxes value-type cases; for a default union Value is null, and if Value may be null the switch must handle null to avoid a warning.

questions.prompt: `IEnumerable<Order> GetPending()` returns a LINQ query over a source that makes a network call per enumeration, and a caller writes `if (orders.Any()) { log.Info(orders.Count()); foreach (var o in orders) ... }`. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The query variable stores the query, not results, so every enumeration runs it again
`Any()`, `Count()` and the `foreach` each enumerate, so the source is called three times
If the source changes between calls, the logged count may not match what the loop sees
`Count()` reuses the result cached by the earlier `Any()` call without running the query
Calling `ToList()` once would still re-run the query on every later `foreach` over the list

questions.explanation: A LINQ query variable holds the instructions, not the data, so each enumeration executes it against the source again. `Any()` and `Count()` execute immediately and each enumerate, and the `foreach` enumerates once more, so this code makes three round trips. Because results reflect the source at execution time, they can differ between enumerations. LINQ doesn't cache between calls; materializing once with `ToList()` or `ToArray()` stores the results, so later loops read the list rather than re-running the query.

sources.title: Introduction to LINQ Queries - C#
sources.claim: The query variable doesn't hold results; deferred queries run when enumerated and results can differ every time if enumerated multiple times; operators returning a scalar such as Count execute immediately (Any is listed as immediate); ToList or ToArray force immediate execution and cache the results.

questions.prompt: A repository method is `IEnumerable<Order> Find(Func<Order, bool> filter) => _ctx.Orders.Where(filter);`, and after launch database CPU and network traffic spike. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: With a `Func`, the filter runs on the client, so every row is pulled from the database first
Taking `Expression<Func<Order, bool>>` lets EF read the filter as a tree and translate it to SQL
A statement lambda with braces can be passed as an `Expression<Func<...>>` like any other
Constructs such as `?.` and interpolated strings aren't allowed inside an expression tree
With an expression filter, EF evaluates any untranslatable method call in `Where` on the client

questions.explanation: A `Func` is compiled code, not data, so `Where` binds to `Enumerable.Where`: EF sends an unfiltered query and the filter runs in memory over every row. Assigning a lambda to `Expression<TDelegate>` builds an expression tree, which EF's `Queryable` APIs translate to SQL. Only expression lambdas become trees, and many constructs, including `?.`, interpolated strings and pattern matching, aren't allowed in them. EF Core only evaluates untranslatable code on the client in the top-level projection; elsewhere, such as in `Where`, it throws at run time.

sources.title: Expression Trees - C#
sources.claim: When a lambda is assigned to Expression<TDelegate>, the compiler builds an expression tree, which lets Entity Framework translate the query into SQL; only expression lambdas can be converted, and constructs such as ?., interpolated strings and pattern matching can't be used.

sources.title: Client vs. Server Evaluation - EF Core
sources.claim: EF Core supports client evaluation only in the top-level projection and throws for untranslatable expressions elsewhere; a filter that can't be applied in the database means all the data must be pulled into memory.

questions.prompt: A team wants to publish a service with Native AOT, but it uses reflection-based System.Text.Json serialization everywhere. Which statements about moving to source generation are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Source generators run at compile time and add code, moving the metadata work out of run time
You declare a `partial` class deriving from `JsonSerializerContext` with `[JsonSerializable]`
Runtime types stored in `object` members must also be listed with `[JsonSerializable]`
The serialization-optimized fast path is also used for async serialization of large payloads
Reflection-based serialization keeps working in Native AOT, so the switch is optional

questions.explanation: Source generators read the compilation and add code to it at build time, so the metadata that reflection used to discover at run time is generated up front. For System.Text.Json you declare a `partial` `JsonSerializerContext` with `[JsonSerializable(typeof(T))]` for each root type, and any runtime type behind an `object` member must be declared too. The fast-path mode isn't supported for async serialization. Native AOT doesn't support the reflection that default serialization needs, so reflection-based code breaks there.

sources.title: The .NET Compiler Platform SDK (Roslyn APIs) - C#
sources.claim: Source generators enable compile-time metaprogramming: code created at compile time and added to the compilation, after reading the contents of the compilation and any additional files.

sources.title: How to use source generation in System.Text.Json - .NET
sources.claim: Create a partial class deriving from JsonSerializerContext with JsonSerializableAttribute; the runtime type of members declared as object must be specified; fast-path serialization isn't supported for asynchronous serialization; reflection-based serialization can break Native AOT apps.

questions.prompt: You inherit a large ASP.NET MVC 5 app on .NET Framework 4.8 with heavy `System.Web` use, shared class libraries, WCF services and session state, and must move it to .NET 10 without a feature freeze. Which steps match Microsoft's guidance? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Migrate incrementally with the Strangler Fig pattern, keeping the app in production
Do an in-place migration, since that suits large apps with heavy `System.Web` use
Upgrade the shared libraries in postorder depth-first order, multi-targeting them
Move the WCF server side to the CoreWCF packages, which run on modern .NET
Keep isolating plugins in separate AppDomains, which .NET 10 still lets you create

questions.explanation: For a large production app with heavy `System.Web` use, Microsoft recommends incremental migration, an implementation of the Strangler Fig pattern; in-place migration suits small apps. Shared libraries are upgraded in postorder depth-first order and multi-targeted so both apps can use them, while cross-cutting concerns such as session and authentication are planned for both apps. WCF server can run on modern .NET through CoreWCF. Creating extra AppDomains isn't supported; use separate processes or containers for isolation.

sources.title: Migrate from ASP.NET Framework to ASP.NET Core
sources.claim: Incremental migration is an implementation of the Strangler Fig pattern, best for large apps that stay in production and recommended for heavy System.Web use; in-place migration suits small apps; libraries must be upgraded in postorder depth-first order and multi-targeted; session state and authentication are cross-cutting concerns.

sources.title: .NET Framework technologies unavailable on .NET 6+
sources.claim: Creating more app domains isn't supported, so use separate processes or containers; WCF server can be used in .NET 6+ through the CoreWCF NuGet packages.

questions.prompt: During a .NET 8 to .NET 10 upgrade, the build fails with ambiguous-call errors on `Where` and `Select` over `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: .NET 10 adds `System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable`, which clashes with the `System.Linq.Async` package
A direct `System.Linq.Async` reference should be removed or upgraded to version 7.0.0
A transitive `System.Linq.Async` can be hidden with `<ExcludeAssets>compile</ExcludeAssets>`
`SelectAwait` calls keep compiling unchanged, because the new API kept that method name
Default .NET 10 container images keep the previous base OS, so Dockerfiles need no review

Remove a direct reference or upgrade it to 7.0.0, and exclude a transitive one with `ExcludeAssets` set to `compile`. Some names changed: `SelectAwait` becomes `Select` with an async lambda. Other .NET 10 changes worth checking include default container images moving to Ubuntu and `dotnet restore` auditing transitive packages.

sources.title: Breaking change - System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable in .NET 10 - .NET

sources.title: Breaking changes in .NET 10

questions.prompt: A team wants to publish an existing ASP.NET Core service with Native AOT to cut cold-start time in serverless containers. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Native AOT gives faster startup and a smaller memory footprint than a JIT-compiled app
MVC, Session, and authentication other than JWT aren't supported under Native AOT
`System.Reflection.Emit` and `Assembly.LoadFile` still work, just more slowly
If publishing shows no AOT warnings, the app should behave like the JIT-compiled one
A Native AOT binary built for Windows also runs on Linux, like a framework-dependent app

questions.explanation: Native AOT apps start faster and use less memory, which helps workloads with many instances. Not every ASP.NET Core feature is supported: MVC, Session and authentication other than JWT aren't. There's no dynamic loading and no runtime code generation, and trimming is required. An app that publishes with AOT warnings might not work correctly, while one with no warnings should behave like the JIT version. Native AOT output targets a specific runtime identifier, such as `linux-x64`.

sources.title: Native AOT deployment overview - .NET
sources.claim: Native AOT apps have faster startup and smaller memory footprints and target a specific runtime environment; limitations include no dynamic loading (Assembly.LoadFile), no runtime code generation (System.Reflection.Emit) and required trimming.

sources.title: ASP.NET Core support for Native AOT
sources.claim: MVC, Session and Other Authentication aren't supported with Native AOT while JWT Authentication is; if no AOT warnings are issued at publish time, the AOT app should work the same as the untrimmed JIT-compiled app.
